description: Enforces exclusive use of FIPS 140-3 validated cryptographic modules for all system cryptographic operations. Enabled via the fips=1 kernel boot parameter (dracut fips module) and fips-mode-setup on RHEL, or FIPSAlgorithmPolicy registry key on Windows. When active, the kernel crypto API restricts to validated implementations (AES, SHA-256+, RSA 2048+, ECDSA P-256/P-384, HMAC), the OpenSSL FIPS provider replaces the default provider, and GnuTLS/NSS restrict to FIPS-approved algorithms. Non-validated algorithms (MD5, RC4, DES, Blowfish, Camellia, IDEA) are removed from available cipher lists entirely — operations requesting them fail with an error rather than falling back to a weaker option. FIPS mode imposes significant compatibility constraints: some TLS cipher suites become unavailable, HMAC-MD5 is prohibited (breaking some Kerberos configurations), Ed25519 SSH keys are rejected, and applications using non-validated crypto (custom OpenSSL builds, BoringSSL, Go's crypto/tls) are unaffected. On RHEL, FIPS mode automatically sets the crypto policy to FIPS, which is stricter than DEFAULT but less restrictive than FUTURE for non-FIPS-relevant parameters. The primary value is compliance attestation (FedRAMP, CMMC, DISA STIG) combined with the security benefit of using audited, CAVP-tested implementations.

cvss_vector_impacts.rationale: Without FIPS mode, system crypto libraries offer both validated and non-validated algorithm implementations — an attacker exploiting a protocol downgrade vulnerability can force negotiation to a non-validated, potentially weaker implementation (e.g., MD5-based HMAC, RC4 stream cipher, DES). With FIPS mode active, non-validated algorithms are removed from the kernel crypto API and userspace library provider lists entirely — the negotiation cannot select them because they do not exist in the available set. The attacker must find an exploitable flaw in the FIPS-validated implementation itself, which has undergone NIST CAVP testing and third-party lab validation. Does not increase complexity for vulnerabilities that do not involve cryptographic algorithm selection (memory corruption, logic bugs, injection)

verification.method: Verify FIPS mode is enabled at boot, kernel, and crypto library levels

remediation.name: Enable FIPS 140-3 mode via fips-mode-setup

steps.description: Enable FIPS mode system-wide (sets fips=1 kernel boot parameter, rebuilds initramfs with dracut fips module, and configures crypto-policies to FIPS). Requires a reboot to take effect.
Reboot to activate FIPS mode (kernel must boot with fips=1 for the crypto API to restrict to validated modules)

remediation.verify: fips-mode-setup --check && cat /proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled && openssl list -providers 2>/dev/null | grep -c fips

references.source: RHEL 9 — Switching the system to FIPS mode

remediation.name: Enable FIPS algorithm policy via registry

steps.description: Enable the FIPS Algorithm Policy registry key (forces Windows CNG and legacy CSP providers to use only FIPS-validated algorithms)
Reboot to activate FIPS policy (CNG providers reload with FIPS restrictions on boot)

relationships.rationale: FIPS mode removes non-validated algorithm implementations from the crypto library provider — applications cannot invoke broken or risky algorithms because they are absent from the loaded module set
FIPS validation requires minimum key sizes (RSA 2048+, ECDSA P-256+, AES-128+) — the validated module enforces these minimums and rejects key generation or import below the threshold
MD5 and SHA-1 for digital signatures are removed from the FIPS provider — hash operations requesting non-approved algorithms fail rather than producing weak hashes
Non-validated algorithms are absent from the negotiation set — protocol downgrade attacks cannot force selection of a weaker algorithm because it does not exist in the library's available ciphers
